citation.title: Information and Access to United Nations Diplomatic Missions

standing_assumptions:
The article is a four-page empirical report of one field experiment (printed pp. 594-597 are PDF pp. 1-4; PDF p. 5 is a copyright notice). It states no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof and uses no potential-outcome notation; its only displayed formula is the regression model in Section III. The setting, as printed (read from the page images):
Population and design (Section II, p. 595, PDF p. 2): “We contacted by email all 189 UN Permanent Missions from member states that had current diplomatic relations with the United States at the time of the intervention.” and “Of the 189 missions contacted, 94 were randomly assigned the peer treatment and 95 the world affairs treatment.” The paper says nothing more about the assignment mechanism; the validators read it as complete randomization of a fixed number of missions (94 of 189) to the peer treatment.
Outcomes (Section II, p. 595, PDF p. 2): “Analysis was conducted with treatment assignment blinded. Our outcome of interest is response to emails. We code separately ‘interest response’ for emails that had some indication of interest, and ‘any response’, for any type of reply to the email, including interest responses, notification of a change in the Permanent Representative and declination to participate. Table 1 shows number and percentage of responses by treatment group.”
Table 1 (p. 595, PDF p. 2), “Response by treatment.”: Peers: Countries 94; Any response, Count 10, Per cent 10.64; Interest response, Count 10, Per cent 10.64. World affairs: Countries 95; Any response, Count 10, Per cent 10.53; Interest response, Count 7, Per cent 7.37. Note: “‘Per cent’ columns represent count as a percentage of countries assigned to respective treatment group. ‘Interest’ responses are a subset of ‘any’ responses.”
Covariates (Section II, Country data, p. 595, PDF p. 2): “We follow Fisman and Miguel (2007) in selection of control variables, and use the replication files for their article as a source for data on these variables (Fisman and Miguel 2015). As expected given randomization, we find no statistically or substantively significant differences in covariate balance between the two groups. For missing covariate entries, we follow Lin, Green, and Coppock (2015) and use mean imputation.”
Estimation (Section III; the display is at the foot of p. 595, PDF p. 2, and the sentence continues at the top of the left column of p. 596, PDF p. 3, below Table 2), as printed: “We conduct an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression of the outcomes on an indicator for assignment to peer treatment. The model we estimate is $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Peers + \boldsymbol{X}\gamma + \epsilon$$ where $\beta_1$ represents the peer assignment indicator, $\boldsymbol{X}$ represents the vector of covariates, including country-level covariates and indicators for region and $\varepsilon$ is a disturbance with $E[\varepsilon|Peers, \boldsymbol{X}] = 0$. Note that, when covariates are not included, this estimator of $\beta_1$ reduces to the well-known difference-in-means.” The display prints the disturbance as $\epsilon$ and the sentence below it prints $\varepsilon$; they are the same object. The clause “where $\beta_1$ represents the peer assignment indicator” is the misprint of finding P036-E001 (see P036-T1). Next paragraph (p. 596): “We first report estimates without covariate adjustment (the difference-in-means), followed by specifications controlling for country-level covariates and indicators for region. Summary results for OLS regressions are presented in Table 2.”
Table 2 (p. 596, PDF p. 3), “Ordinary least squares regressions: any response.”: columns (1), (2), (3) under “Any response” and (4), (5), (6) under “Interest response”. Treatment effect: 0.001, $-0.010$, $-0.001$, 0.033, 0.023, 0.033, with (0.045), (0.045), (0.046), (0.042), (0.042), (0.043) in parentheses below. Control mean: 0.105, 0.111, 0.106, 0.074, 0.078, 0.074, with (0.032), (0.033), (0.033), (0.027), (0.028), (0.028) below. Country characteristics: No, Yes, Yes, No, Yes, Yes. Region indicators: No, No, Yes, No, No, Yes. Note: “‘Any response’ indicator is the dependent variable for specifications 1, 2 and 3. ‘Interest response’ indicator is the dependent variable for specifications 4, 5 and 6. Heteroscedasticity-consistent SEs are reported in parentheses, using MacKinnon and White (1985) HC2 estimators; these estimators are generally conservative under a randomization model (Samii and Aronow 2012). ‘Country characteristics’ indicates inclusion of country-level covariates in the specification. Covariates are number of diplomats in the UN mission, corruption index, log per capita income, average government wage divided by per capita income, log weighted distance between country and US populations, log total trade with the USA and dummies for whether the country received US economic aid and US military aid. ‘Region indicators’ are dummy variables for the region in which the country is located: Africa, Asia, Europe, South America or the Middle East; North America is the excluded region.”
Scope of the targets. None of the headline claims P036-H1 to P036-H6 is a mathematical statement: H1 to H4 are empirical estimates and statements about their statistical significance, H5 describes the population contacted, and H6 is an interpretive remark; so there is no headline target. The four confirmed errors are all rated Minor, so there is no result_touched_by_finding target, and no validator gave a counterexample to a printed statement, so there is no counterexample target. Two confirmed errors have a correction that changes a mathematical statement and each gets a corrected-statement target: P036-E001 (the coefficient $\beta_1$ named as the assignment indicator in the sentence that defines the terms of the regression model) and P036-N003 (the conservativeness of the HC2 standard errors, attributed for all six columns of Table 2 to a paper that proves it for the regression without covariates only). Not targets: P036-E002 (the title of Table 2 names one of its two outcomes) and P036-E003 (‘authors(s)’ and a citation year), whose corrections change no mathematical statement; P036-N005 (a clarity note); P036-N001, P036-N008 and P036-N009 (not confirmed; the exact countermodels in the P036-N001 artifact concern estimands that Sol found the paper does not claim); P036-N002, P036-N004, P036-N006 and P036-N007 (undetermined).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section III, the regression model and the sentence defining its terms (“where $\beta_1$ represents the peer assignment indicator”), corrected: $Peers$ is the indicator and $\beta_1$ its coefficient, whose OLS estimator without covariates is the difference in means
canonical_claim.location: pp. 595-596 (PDF pp. 2-3): the display at the foot of the right column of p. 595; the defining sentence at the top of the left column of p. 596, below Table 2
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; Section III, foot of p. 595 and top of p. 596] “We conduct an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression of the outcomes on an indicator for assignment to peer treatment. The model we estimate is $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Peers + \boldsymbol{X}\gamma + \epsilon$$ where $\beta_1$ represents the peer assignment indicator, $\boldsymbol{X}$ represents the vector of covariates, including country-level covariates and indicators for region and $\varepsilon$ is a disturbance with $E[\varepsilon|Peers, \boldsymbol{X}] = 0$. Note that, when covariates are not included, this estimator of $\beta_1$ reduces to the well-known difference-in-means.”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, verbatim: “Replace “where $\beta_1$ represents the peer assignment indicator” with “where $Peers$ represents the peer assignment indicator”.”] “We conduct an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression of the outcomes on an indicator for assignment to peer treatment. The model we estimate is $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Peers + \boldsymbol{X}\gamma + \epsilon$$ where $Peers$ represents the peer assignment indicator, $\boldsymbol{X}$ represents the vector of covariates, including country-level covariates and indicators for region and $\varepsilon$ is a disturbance with $E[\varepsilon|Peers, \boldsymbol{X}] = 0$. Note that, when covariates are not included, this estimator of $\beta_1$ reduces to the well-known difference-in-means.”
[The same correction in the fuller wording that Sol accepted as correct (validated.json, P036-E001, prior_correction.corrected_text), verbatim] “$Peers$ is an indicator equal to one for assignment to the peer treatment and zero for assignment to the world-affairs treatment; $\beta_1$ is its coefficient.”
[Mathematical content of the corrected passage, with every hypothesis] Units $i=1,\dots,n$ (the paper has $n=189$ missions) have outcomes $Y_i\in\mathbb{R}$ and assignment indicators $Peers_i\in\{0,1\}$, equal to $1$ for assignment to the peer treatment and $0$ for assignment to the world affairs treatment. Write $n_1=\sum_i Peers_i$ and $n_0=n-n_1$ and assume $n_1\ge 1$ and $n_0\ge 1$. Let $\bar Y_1=n_1^{-1}\sum_{i:Peers_i=1}Y_i$ and $\bar Y_0=n_0^{-1}\sum_{i:Peers_i=0}Y_i$. (i) Roles of the symbols. $Peers$ is the regressor, a $\{0,1\}$-valued variable; $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are real coefficients and $\gamma$ is a real coefficient vector; $\beta_1$ multiplies $Peers$. If $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1 Peers+\boldsymbol{X}\gamma+\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon$ and $\boldsymbol{X}\gamma$ integrable and $E[\varepsilon|Peers,\boldsymbol{X}]=0$, then $E[Y|Peers,\boldsymbol{X}]=\beta_0+\beta_1 Peers+\boldsymbol{X}\gamma$ almost surely; in the model without covariates, $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1 Peers+\varepsilon$ with $E[\varepsilon|Peers]=0$ and $0<P(Peers=1)<1$, this gives $E[Y|Peers=1]-E[Y|Peers=0]=\beta_1$ and $E[Y|Peers=0]=\beta_0$. (ii) “when covariates are not included, this estimator of $\beta_1$ reduces to the well-known difference-in-means”: the function $(b_0,b_1)\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-b_0-b_1 Peers_i)^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ has a unique minimizer $(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)$, and $$\hat\beta_1=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0,\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar Y_0 .$$ (iii) The paper's two instances, from the counts of Table 1 ($n_1=94$, $n_0=95$, binary outcomes): for ‘any response’, $\hat\beta_1=\tfrac{10}{94}-\tfrac{10}{95}=\tfrac{1}{893}$ and $\hat\beta_0=\tfrac{10}{95}=\tfrac{2}{19}$; for ‘interest response’, $\hat\beta_1=\tfrac{10}{94}-\tfrac{7}{95}=\tfrac{146}{4465}$ and $\hat\beta_0=\tfrac{7}{95}$. Rounded to three decimals these are the entries $0.001$, $0.105$ of Table 2, column (1), and $0.033$, $0.074$ of column (4).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. $Y$: ‘the outcomes’ (p. 595), that is the ‘any response’ indicator in specifications 1, 2 and 3 and the ‘interest response’ indicator in specifications 4, 5 and 6 (note to Table 2, p. 596); both are defined in Section II, p. 595 (transcribed under standing_assumptions). $Peers$: after the correction, ‘the peer assignment indicator’ (p. 596), ‘an indicator for assignment to peer treatment’ (p. 595); the two arms are in Section II, p. 595: “Of the 189 missions contacted, 94 were randomly assigned the peer treatment and 95 the world affairs treatment.” $\boldsymbol{X}$: ‘the vector of covariates, including country-level covariates and indicators for region’ (p. 596), listed in the note to Table 2. $\varepsilon$ (printed $\epsilon$ in the display): ‘a disturbance with $E[\varepsilon|Peers,\boldsymbol{X}]=0$’ (p. 596). ‘This estimator of $\beta_1$’: the OLS coefficient on $Peers$ (‘an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression’, p. 595; ‘the coefficient on the peer assignment indicator in the unadjusted regression (1)’, p. 596). ‘Difference-in-means’: not defined by a formula; the paper identifies it with the difference between the two ‘Per cent’ entries of Table 1 (p. 596: “As this is a simple difference-in-means, this is also reflected in the ‘Per cent’ column under the ‘Any response’ treatment in Table 1.”), that is $\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0$ with the arm means defined in the statement.
Not defined in the paper and supplied here: $\beta_0$ (the intercept; Table 2 reports it in the row ‘Control mean’), $\gamma$ (the coefficient vector of $\boldsymbol{X}$), the unit index $i$, the arm sizes $n_1$, $n_0$ and the arm means $\bar Y_1$, $\bar Y_0$, and the definition of the OLS estimator as the minimizer of the residual sum of squares.
canonical_claim.note: Finding P036-E001 is rated Minor (class error; the merge records its kind as notation). Sol's verdict is confirmed, with the intended meaning clear from context and nothing depending on the clause. The validation is a page check, recorded in runs/P036/validate/_batch/P036-B01/verdicts.json; there is no derivation and no counterexample, because the defect is a substituted symbol and not a false proposition with a witness: as printed, the coefficient $\beta_1$ is named as the indicator, which leaves the regressor $Peers$ without a definition and leaves ‘this estimator of $\beta_1$’ in the next sentence referring to an estimator of an indicator. The paper itself uses the corrected roles two paragraphs later (p. 596: ‘the coefficient on the peer assignment indicator in the unadjusted regression (1)’). What a Lean statement should carry is the typing in (i) (the indicator is a $\{0,1\}$-valued variable on units, $\beta_1$ a real number that multiplies it) and the identity (ii); the conditional-mean lines in (i) are one-step consequences of the printed assumption on the disturbance and (iii) is arithmetic. Parts (i) to (iii) are this list's reading of the corrected passage in the paper's own terms; (ii) is the paper's own sentence, which both readers and the reproduction checked (candidates.json, held_up: ‘The statement that OLS without covariates reduces to the difference in means is correct and matches the numbers’). The rational values in (iii) were recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed. P036-T2 reuses (ii). The merge lists the finding as a related candidate of P036-H3; the rater records no headline claim as affected.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Table 2, note, third sentence (the HC2 standard errors “are generally conservative under a randomization model (Samii and Aronow 2012)”), restricted to specifications (1) and (4): the HC2 variance estimator equals the Neyman estimator and is conservative in expectation under complete randomization
canonical_claim.location: p. 596 (PDF p. 3), note to Table 2, third sentence
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; note to Table 2, third sentence; it applies to the standard errors in parentheses in all six columns, of which (2), (3), (5) and (6) include covariates] “Heteroscedasticity-consistent SEs are reported in parentheses, using MacKinnon and White (1985) HC2 estimators; these estimators are generally conservative under a randomization model (Samii and Aronow 2012).”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, verbatim] “Restrict the cited justification to unadjusted specifications: 'HC2 standard errors are reported; for specifications (1) and (4), the corresponding variance estimator is conservative in expectation under complete randomization (Samii and Aronow 2012).' An adjusted-regression justification would require a separate appropriate result and its conditions.”
[Mathematical content of the corrected sentence, with every hypothesis; from the validator's derivation.md, sections 1 and 2] Setting. $N$ units $i=1,\dots,N$ with fixed potential outcomes $Y_i(1),Y_i(0)\in\mathbb{R}$. Integers $n_1\ge 2$ and $n_0\ge 2$ with $n_1+n_0=N$. Complete randomization: the set of treated units is uniformly distributed over the $\binom{N}{n_1}$ subsets of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ of size $n_1$; $T_i\in\{0,1\}$ indicates that unit $i$ is treated, and the observed outcome is $Y_i=Y_i(T_i)$. Every expectation and variance below is over this assignment alone. Population quantities: $\mu_w=N^{-1}\sum_i Y_i(w)$ and $S_w^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_i (Y_i(w)-\mu_w)^2$ for $w\in\{0,1\}$; $\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)$, $\bar\tau=\mu_1-\mu_0$ and $S_\tau^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_i(\tau_i-\bar\tau)^2$. Sample quantities: $\bar Y_1=n_1^{-1}\sum_{i:T_i=1}Y_i$, $\bar Y_0=n_0^{-1}\sum_{i:T_i=0}Y_i$, $s_1^2=(n_1-1)^{-1}\sum_{i:T_i=1}(Y_i-\bar Y_1)^2$ and $s_0^2=(n_0-1)^{-1}\sum_{i:T_i=0}(Y_i-\bar Y_0)^2$. Regression without covariates (specifications (1) and (4)): ordinary least squares of $Y_i$ on $D_i=(1,T_i)'$, with $D'D=\sum_i D_iD_i'=\begin{pmatrix}N&n_1\\ n_1&n_1\end{pmatrix}$, coefficient vector $(\hat\alpha,\hat\tau)'=(D'D)^{-1}\sum_i D_iY_i$, residuals $e_i=Y_i-\hat\alpha-\hat\tau T_i$ and leverages $h_i=D_i'(D'D)^{-1}D_i$. The HC2 covariance matrix is $(D'D)^{-1}\big(\sum_i \tfrac{e_i^2}{1-h_i}D_iD_i'\big)(D'D)^{-1}$, and $\hat V_{HC2}$ denotes its diagonal entry for the coefficient on $T$. Claims. (a) For every assignment, $\hat\tau=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0$ and $\hat\alpha=\bar Y_0$; $h_i=1/n_1$ if $T_i=1$ and $h_i=1/n_0$ if $T_i=0$. (b) For every assignment, $$\hat V_{HC2}=\sum_{i:T_i=1}\frac{e_i^2}{n_1^2(1-1/n_1)}+\sum_{i:T_i=0}\frac{e_i^2}{n_0^2(1-1/n_0)}=\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_0^2}{n_0},$$ the Neyman variance estimator. (c) $E[\hat\tau]=\mu_1-\mu_0$ and $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau)=\frac{S_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{S_0^2}{n_0}-\frac{S_\tau^2}{N}.$$ (d) $E[s_1^2]=S_1^2$ and $E[s_0^2]=S_0^2$, hence $$E[\hat V_{HC2}]-\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau)=\frac{S_\tau^2}{N}\ \ge\ 0,$$ with equality if and only if $\tau_i$ is the same for every unit. This is the sense of ‘conservative in expectation’. (e) The paper's two instances ($N=189$, $n_1=94$, $n_0=95$; for a binary outcome with $k$ ones among $n$ observations the sample variance is $k(n-k)/[n(n-1)]$): specification (1), ‘any response’, counts $10$ and $10$: $\hat V_{HC2}=\tfrac{10\cdot 84}{94^2\cdot 93}+\tfrac{10\cdot 85}{95^2\cdot 94}=\tfrac{50039}{24720919}$, whose square root is $0.04499\ldots$ (printed $0.045$); specification (4), ‘interest response’, counts $10$ and $7$: $\hat V_{HC2}=\tfrac{10\cdot 84}{94^2\cdot 93}+\tfrac{7\cdot 88}{95^2\cdot 94}=\tfrac{1080506}{618022975}$, whose square root is $0.04181\ldots$ (printed $0.042$). Not asserted by the corrected sentence: that the realized $\hat V_{HC2}$ is at least $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau)$ for every assignment; that $E[\sqrt{\hat V_{HC2}}]\ge\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau)}$; or any property of the standard errors of the specifications with covariates, (2), (3), (5) and (6).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The six specifications and their standard errors: Table 2, p. 596 (PDF p. 3), transcribed under standing_assumptions; specifications (1) and (4) are the two with ‘Country characteristics: No’ and ‘Region indicators: No’, that is the regression of the outcome on an intercept and the peer assignment indicator alone (‘the unadjusted regression (1)’, ‘the unadjusted regression (4)’, p. 596). The design: “Of the 189 missions contacted, 94 were randomly assigned the peer treatment and 95 the world affairs treatment.” (p. 595, PDF p. 2). The counts used in (e): Table 1, p. 595. The estimator for (1) and (4): P036-T1, part (ii).
Not defined in the paper. ‘HC2’ is given only by the citation of MacKinnon and White (1985); ‘a randomization model’ and ‘conservative’ are not defined; the paper has no potential-outcome notation. Supplied by the validator (runs/P036/validate/P036-N003/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 1 and 2): the fixed potential outcomes $Y_i(1)$, $Y_i(0)$; complete randomization of exactly $n_1$ of $N$ units, uniform over subsets, with $n_1,n_0>1$; the population variances $S_1^2$, $S_0^2$, $S_\tau^2$ with divisor $N-1$; the sample variances $s_1^2$, $s_0^2$ with divisor $n_w-1$; the design matrix rows $D_i=(1,T_i)$, the leverages, and the HC2 sandwich with squared residuals divided by $1-h_i$; ‘conservative in expectation’ as $E[\hat V_{HC2}]\ge\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau)$ over the assignment. The external source check (runs/P036/settle/settled.json, P036-N003) reports that the same setting and regression are those of Samii and Aronow (2012): complete randomization with fixed potential outcomes (their p. 366), a regression on an intercept and a treatment indicator only (p. 367, equation 4), and Theorem 1 with Corollary 1 for the HC2/Neyman equivalence and conservativeness in expectation.
canonical_claim.note: Finding P036-N003 is rated Minor (class error; the merge records its kind as citation); Sol's verdict is confirmed_in_part, with repair cost weaker_conclusion. What is confirmed is the scope of the attribution: the cited paper proves the property for the regression on an intercept and a treatment indicator, which covers columns (1) and (4) and not the covariate-adjusted columns. The printed hedged sentence is not shown false: Sol records false_under_natural_reading as false and reports no counterexample to it (‘A mathematical counterexample to the hedged natural reading’ is listed under what is not established), so there is no counterexample target, and a proof of this target does not refute the printed sentence; it proves the statement that the citation supports. The target is included because the correction narrows a mathematical statement (which estimators, in which sense, under which design) and the author requires a formalization of the corrected version of every confirmed mathematical error. Claims (a) to (d) are exact finite-population statements: (a) and (b) are identities for each assignment, (c) and (d) are finite sums over the $\binom{N}{n_1}$ assignments; (a) repeats P036-T1 (ii) with $Peers=T$. The validator's check.py verifies the inverse matrix, the weights, the leverages and (b) symbolically, and reproduces (e); the rational values in (e) were recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed, with HC2 computed from the sandwich formula and not from the closed form. A small test instance, from the second checker (P036-N003/recheck-v1/independent_check.py): $N=6$, $n_1=3$, $Y(1)=(0,1,1,0,1,0)$, $Y(0)=(1,0,1,0,0,0)$ gives $E[\hat V_{HC2}]=17/90$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau)=17/180$ and $S_\tau^2/N=17/180$ over the 20 assignments; it checks the identity in (d) and is not a counterexample to anything. Not part of this target. (1) The ‘Control mean’ row: by the same identities the HC2 diagonal entry for the intercept is $s_0^2/n_0$ (in the paper's instances $17/16967$ and $308/424175$, square roots $0.0317$ and $0.0269$, printed $0.032$ and $0.027$), with $E[s_0^2/n_0]-\mathrm{Var}(\bar Y_0)=S_0^2/N\ge 0$ since $\mathrm{Var}(\bar Y_0)=(1/n_0-1/N)S_0^2$; this is an optional corollary, outside the cited theorem. (2) The covariate-adjusted columns: section 3 of the validator's derivation argues that HC2 is conservative to first order asymptotically for the additive regression under regularity conditions that the paper does not state (a fixed number of covariates, bounded arrays, $n_1/N\to p\in(0,1)$, a covariate second-moment matrix bounded away from singularity). Sol's repair does not assert it (‘An adjusted-regression justification would require a separate appropriate result and its conditions’), so it is not a target. No headline claim lists this finding as related and the rater records none as affected; the standard errors of columns (1) and (4) are the ones behind the non-significance statement of P036-H3.
